content:
Hello All

I have been formalizing online convex optimization regret proofs. Mathlib has many useful results for this but misses results on Bregman divergences and convex subgradients (maybe Fenchel conjugates) which I have been formalizing as needed.

I am following the steps from https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/how-to-contribute.html to try and contribute this to Mathlib.

I choose to define a generalized form of a Bregman divergence which then convex subgradient on a constraint set V is defined through and inherits most of the properties of. Concretely: 

import Mathlib.Algebra.Group.Hom.Defs
import Mathlib.Algebra.Module.Basic
import Mathlib.Algebra.Order.Group.Defs
import Mathlib.Algebra.Order.Ring.Defs
import Mathlib.Algebra.Order.Module.Basic
import Mathlib.Order.ConditionallyCompleteLattice.Basic
import Mathlib.Tactic

variable {E F : Type*} [AddCommGroup E] [AddCommGroup F]

section Bregman

@[local simp]
def bregmanDivergenceVal (f : E → F) (x y : E) (J : E →+ F) : F :=
  f x - f y - J (x - y)

syntax "D_[" term "](" term ", " term ", " term ")" : term
macro_rules
| `(D_[$f:term]($x:term, $y:term, $J:term)) => `(bregmanDivergenceVal $f $x $y $J)

@[app_unexpander bregmanDivergenceVal]
def unexpandBregmanDivergenceVal : Lean.PrettyPrinter.Unexpander
  | `($_ $f $x $y $J) => `(D_[$f]($x, $y, $J))
  | _                 => throw ()

@[simp]
lemma bregmanDivergenceVal_self (f : E → F) (x : E) (J_x : E →+ F) :
    D_[f](x, x, J_x) = 0 := by simp

@[simp]
lemma bregmanDivergenceVal_add (f₁ f₂ : E → F) (x y : E) (J₁ J₂ : E →+ F) :
    D_[f₁ + f₂](x, y, J₁ + J₂) = D_[f₁](x, y, J₁) + D_[f₂](x, y, J₂) := by
  simp only [bregmanDivergenceVal, Pi.add_apply, AddMonoidHom.add_apply, map_sub]
  abel

end Bregman


variable [PartialOrder F]

def IsSubgradient (V : Set E) (f : E → F) (y : E) (g_y : E →+ F) : Prop :=
  y ∈ V ∧ ∀ x ∈ V, 0 ≤ D_[f](x, y, g_y)

def Subdiff (V : Set E) (f : E → F) (y : E) : Set (E →+ F) :=
  { g | IsSubgradient V f y g }

notation:60 "∂[" V ", " y "] " f:50 => Subdiff V f y

@[app_unexpander Subdiff]
def unexpandSubdiff : Lean.PrettyPrinter.Unexpander
  | `($_ $V $f $y) => `(∂[$V, $y] $f)
  | _              => throw ()

variable {V : Set E} {f : E → F} {y x : E} {g_y : E →+ F}

@[local simp]
lemma mem_subdiff_iff : g_y ∈ ∂[V, y] f ↔ y ∈ V ∧ ∀ x ∈ V, 0 ≤ D_[f](x, y, g_y) := Iff.rfl

lemma zero_mem_subdiff_iff :
    0 ∈ ∂[V, y] f ↔ y ∈ V ∧ ∀ x ∈ V, 0 ≤ f x - f y := by simp [bregmanDivergenceVal]

section OrderedGroup
variable [IsOrderedAddMonoid F]

lemma IsSubgradient.add {f₁ f₂ : E → F} {g₁ g₂ : E →+ F}
    (h₁ : g₁ ∈ ∂[V, y] f₁) (h₂ : g₂ ∈ ∂[V, y] f₂) :
    (g₁ + g₂) ∈ ∂[V, y] (f₁ + f₂) :=
  ⟨h₁.1, fun x hx ↦ by simp [add_nonneg (h₁.2 x hx) (h₂.2 x hx)]⟩
end OrderedGroup

Most of subgradient properties follow from Bregman divergence properties which almost follow directly with simp, ring and linarith. I would start by adding these results to Mathlib. If this goes well, move to Fenchel conjugate results which are a bit more tricky. And then bridge to Frechet derivates: 

variable {E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E]
variable {F : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace ℝ F] [PartialOrder F] [IsOrderedAddMonoid F] [OrderClosedTopology F] [PosSMulMono ℝ F]

lemma subgradient_of_hasFDerivAt {f : E → F} {V : Set E} {x : E} {g : E →L[ℝ] F}
    (h_conv : ConvexOn ℝ V f) (hx : x ∈ V)
    (h_deriv : HasFDerivAt f g x) :
    g.toAddMonoidHom ∈ ∂[V, x] f := by sorry

theorem bregmanDivergence_taylor (ψ : E → ℝ) (gradΨ : E → (E →L[ℝ] ℝ)) (x y : E)
    (hgrad : ∀ z ∈ segment ℝ x y, HasFDerivAt ψ (gradΨ z) z)
    (hessΨ : E → (E →L[ℝ] (E →L[ℝ] ℝ)))
    (hHess : ∀ z ∈ segment ℝ x y, HasFDerivAt gradΨ (hessΨ z) z) :
    ∃ z ∈ segment ℝ x y,
      D_[ψ](x, y, (gradΨ y).toAddMonoidHom) = (1/2 : ℝ) * (hessΨ z (x - y)) (x - y) := by sorry

Not sure what results already in Mathlib this would generalize maybe the KL divergence.

Would this be welcomed in Mathlib or what would be the best way to make this reusable for others?

(I use DeepSeek v4 Flash and gemini 3.1 pro and 3.5 3.6 flash in opencode and antigravity while coding)

Thank you
Isidoor

I think the right way to generalize my previous definition of subgradients is:

/-- The subgradient condition states that the Bregman divergence function
`y ↦ D_[f](y, x, g)` belongs to cone `K`. -/
def IsConeSubgradient (K : Set (E → F)) (f : E → F) (x : E) (g : E →+ F) : Prop :=
  (fun y ↦ D_[f](y, x, g)) ∈ K

/-- The subdifferential of `f` at `x` with respect to cone `K`. -/
def ConeSubdiff (K : Set (E → F)) (f : E → F) (x : E) : Set (E →+ F) :=
  { g | IsConeSubgradient K f x g }

I introduce cones which then define subgradients, using cone traits + Bregman divergence properties lift to subgradient properties. All of the subgradients I know from nonsmooth analysis have their own cone. 

-- Cones lift addition K+K = K to subgradients automatically:
theorem IsConeSubgradient.add [IsAddCone K] (h₁ : g₁ ∈ ∂_[K, x] f₁) (h₂ : g₂ ∈ ∂_[K, x] f₂) :
    (g₁ + g₂) ∈ ∂_[K, x] (f₁ + f₂)

Moreover, you can define abstract cones that classify them, abstract constructors, or transform them:
Limiting versions of cones (e.g. the Mordukhovich cone is an outer limit of the Fréchet cone), Convexifications, dual cones, symmetrizations, closures, adding cones, intersections.

All these operations have relationships to each other (most closure types distribute over intersections (and some of them over addition) and inclusions) and lift directly to properties of subgradients. For example, taking an outer limit of a cone automatically transfers properties of the underlying cones and always gives a closed cone (in metric spaces) lifting to a closed subgradient.

One of the most general cones with useful properties (capturing Dini, Fréchet, Clarke) is the asymptotic variation cone builder:

/-!
# Asymptotic Lower Bound Variation Cones
This captures Clarke, Dini, Fréchet, Horizon, and continuity variation cones,
providing their cone closure properties (`IsZeroCone`, `IsAddCone`, `IsSMulCone`)
and inclusion monotonicity in one unified place for scalar and vector-valued variations.
-/

/-- The universal asymptotic lower-bound variation cone:
variations whose linear evaluation `L h` along filter `F_filt` is asymptotically bounded below by `- ε • w`. -/
def AsymptoticCone (E : Type*) {F : Type*}
    [AddCommGroup F] [Preorder F] [Module ℝ F]
    (F_filt : Filter α) (w : α → F) (L : (E → F) →ₗ[ℝ] (α → F)) : Set (E → F) :=
  { h | ∀ (ε : ℝ) (_ : 0 < ε), ∀ᶠ p in F_filt, - ε • w p ≤ L h p }

/-- Trait asserting that a variation cone `K` is realized asymptotically
along filter `F_filt` with weight `w` under linear evaluation `L`. -/
class IsAsymptoticCone (K : Set (E → F))
    (F_filt : outParam (Filter α)) (w : outParam (α → F)) (L : outParam ((E → F) →ₗ[ℝ] (α → F))) : Prop where
  mem_iff : ∀ h, h ∈ K ↔ ∀ (ε : ℝ) (_ : 0 < ε), ∀ᶠ p in F_filt, - ε • w p ≤ L h p

Cones are very general objects: for example, there are cones associated with lower semicontinuity, convexity, star-convexity, quasiconvexity, etc. This allows us to state important results in terms of cones directly, e.g.:

frechetSubCone∩ConvexCone⊆posCone\text{frechetSubCone} \cap \text{ConvexCone} \subseteq \text{posCone}frechetSubCone∩ConvexCone⊆posCone

which directly implies that if 0∈∂Freˊchetf0 \in \partial_{\text{Fréchet}} f0∈∂Freˊchet​f and fff is convex, then 0∈∂globalf  ⟹  0 \in \partial_{\text{global}} f \implies0∈∂global​f⟹ global minimizer.

I haven't worked out all details yet, but I think a lot of statements in nonsmooth analysis can be made purely with cones. (note that this approach is different from using normal cones etc)
